theme_report <- function(base_size = 13) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "#fcfcfb", colour = NA),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#e1e0d9", linewidth = 0.4),
      axis.line.x      = element_line(colour = "#c3c2b7", linewidth = 0.4),
      axis.ticks       = element_blank(),
      text             = element_text(colour = "#52514e"),
      plot.title       = element_text(colour = "#0b0b0b", face = "bold", size = base_size + 2),
      plot.subtitle    = element_text(colour = "#52514e", size = base_size - 1),
      plot.caption     = element_text(colour = "#898781", size = base_size - 3, hjust = 0),
      legend.position  = "top",
      legend.title     = element_blank(),
      strip.text       = element_text(colour = "#0b0b0b", face = "bold")
    )
}

fmt_n   <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "n/a", format(round(x), big.mark = ","))
fmt_pct <- function(x, d = 1) ifelse(is.na(x), "", sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), x))
fmt_sgn <- function(x, d = 1) ifelse(is.na(x), "", sprintf(paste0("%+.", d, "f"), x))
# Serbian number formats (decimal comma)
fmt_d_sr <- function(x, d = 1) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ".", decimal.mark = ",")

# short agency label for charts: drop "(for …)" and other parentheticals
short_agency <- function(a, sr = FALSE) {
  a <- gsub(" \\([^)]*\\)", "", a)
  a <- sub("^Poll attributed to Ipsos Strategic Marketing$", if (sr) "pripisano Ipsosu SM" else "attributed to Ipsos SM", a)
  a <- sub("^ABC News / Washington Post$", "ABC News/WaPo", a)
  a
}

kable_report <- function(df, ..., align = NULL) {
  if (is.null(align)) {
    looks_num <- vapply(df, function(x) is.numeric(x) ||
                          all(grepl("^[-−+]?[0-9.,%× ]*$|<sup>|^$", as.character(x)) & !all(is.na(x)) & any(grepl("[0-9]", x))),
                        logical(1))
    align <- ifelse(looks_num, "r", "l")
  }
  kableExtra::kbl(df, ..., align = align, escape = FALSE) |>
    kableExtra::kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                              full_width = TRUE, position = "center")
}

# Sažetak za javnost {.unnumbered}

<div class="sr">

**Pitanje.** Završna anketa agencije Ipsos Strategic Marketing (objavljena 22. oktobra 2026, n = 3.624) promašila je rezultat parlamentarnih izbora u Srbiji 25. oktobra 2026. za 13,0 poena na *Studentskoj listi* i 8,4 poena na listi *Aleksandar Vučić – Ujedinjena Srbija*, i to u pravcu koji je obrnuo pobednika. U [prethodnom izveštaju](Ipsos-Izbori-2026-SR.html) pokazali smo da slučajna greška uzorka ne može da objasni taj promašaj. Ovde postavljamo drugo pitanje: **koliko je ovaj promašaj veliki u poređenju sa najpoznatijim promašajima predizbornih anketa u svetu od 2010. godine?**

**Šta smo uradili.** Sastavili smo katalog od `r nrow(misses)` dobro dokumentovanih promašaja završnih predizbornih anketa (izbori i referendumi, 2010–2026, širom sveta), uključujući Brexit, američke izbore 2016. i 2020, britanske izbore 2015, 2017. i 2024, kolumbijski referendum o miru 2016, grčki referendum 2015, i anketu pripisanu Ipsosu pred drugi krug predsedničkih izbora u Srbiji 2012. (Tadić – Nikolić). Za svaki slučaj navodimo: šta je anketa objavila, šta su birači uradili, i šta su naknadne analize (zvanične istrage, naučni radovi, izjave samih agencija) ponudile kao objašnjenje. **Svaki broj i svaka tvrdnja imaju referencu** (odeljak [References](#references)).

**Kako merimo promašaj.** Standardna mera u literaturi je *greška razlike*: koliko je anketa promašila **razliku između pobednika i drugoplasiranog**, u procentnim poenima. Na primer, Ipsos je 2026. imao *Ujedinjenu Srbiju* ispred *Studentske liste* za 7,4 poena; stvarna razlika bila je 14,0 poena u korist *Studentske liste*. Greška razlike je zato 7,4 + 14,0 = **21,4 poena**. Pored toga računamo i *standardizovanu grešku*: grešku razlike podeljenu sa statističkom greškom koju bi slučajan uzorak te veličine imao — koliko „standardnih devijacija“ je anketa udaljena od istine. To je ista logika kao u prethodnom izveštaju, u pojednostavljenom obliku (dve liste umesto svih devetnaest).

Narandžasto: Ipsos Strategic Marketing, Srbija (2026, i anketa iz 2012. pripisana Ipsosu). Plavo: druge Ipsos agencije. Sivo: ostale agencije. ✕ = anketa je imala pogrešnog pobednika. **Šta slike pokazuju.**

- Po *sirovoj* grešci razlike, Ipsos 2026. (`r fmt_d_sr(rs26$absE)` poena) je **`r r26_abs`. najveći promašaj** u katalogu od `r nrow(misses)` slučajeva i **`r r26_abs_e`. najveći među izborima** (za razliku od referenduma). Veći su: kolumbijski plebiscit o miru 2016. (Ipsos Napoleón Franco: `r fmt_d_sr(misses$absE[misses$id=="co16"])` poena, izlaznost upola manja od pretpostavljene), grčki referendum 2015. (Public Issue: `r fmt_d_sr(misses$absE[misses$id=="gr15"])`), i dve završne ankete pred drugi krug predsedničkih izbora u Kostariki 2018. — OPol (`r fmt_d_sr(misses$absE[misses$id=="cr18a"])`; anketa koju je, kako se kasnije saznalo, naručio štab kandidata koji je izgubio) i nezavisni univerzitetski CIEP-UCR (`r fmt_d_sr(misses$absE[misses$id=="cr18b"])`), u trci u kojoj je panel istog univerziteta posle izbora utvrdio da je 60% apstinenata iz prvog kruga glasalo za pobednika. Medijana promašaja ostalih redova — a to su redovi izabrani *zato što* su čuveni promašaji — iznosi `r fmt_d_sr(med_abs)` poena; Ipsos 2026. je `r fmt_d_sr(rs26$absE/med_abs)` puta toliko.
- Po *standardizovanoj* grešci — koja uzima u obzir da anketa od 3.600 ispitanika „nema pravo“ na grešku koju ima anketa od 600 — Ipsos 2026. je **`r z_rank_sr` od `r nrow(rank_z)`** (z = `r fmt_d_sr(rs26$z)` sa efektivnom veličinom uzorka od 2.110, izvedenom iz Ipsosovih objavljenih raspona greške; `r fmt_d_sr(z26_nominal)` sa nominalnih 3.624), u društvu: `r paste(case_name_sr(top5_z_others), collapse = ", ")`. Slučajevi koji su, kao Ipsos 2026, u prvih pet i po sirovoj i po standardizovanoj meri: `r both_top5_sr`.
- Ipsos 2026. je takođe **promašio pobednika**, što je u katalogu slučaj u `r round(100 * share_wrong)`% redova, i promašio udeo *Studentske liste* za 13,0 poena — šest puta više od sopstvenog objavljenog raspona greške (±2,1 poena): stvarni udeo *Studentske liste* bio je 10,9 poena iznad gornje granice Ipsosovog intervala.
- **Ipsos nije bio usamljen, ali je među oktobarskim anketama bio najdalje.** U oktobru 2026. samo je još jedna agencija objavila brojke: NSPM (terensko istraživanje 25. 9.–5. 10, n = 1.050, o sopstvenom trošku) imao je *Studentsku listu* ispred, 44,5 prema 42,7 — tačan pobednik, razlika potcenjena za 12 poena. Faktor plus (16.–20. 9, n = 986, naručilac nenaveden) imao je *Ujedinjenu Srbiju* ispred 48,6 prema 37,1 — promašaj od 25,5 poena, ali pet nedelja pred izbore. Procene CRTA-e (jun) i modela BIRODI (avgust) bile su u granicama pet poena od stvarne razlike. Ipsos je, dakle, anketa sa najsvežijim terenom i najvećim uzorkom; veću grešku imala je samo anketa Faktor plus, pet nedelja pred izbore (odeljak 3.5).
- Najčešća objašnjenja u dokumentovanim istragama su: nereprezentativni uzorci koje ponderisanje nije popravilo (Velika Britanija 2015, Australija 2019), neodgovaranje i prikrivanje opredeljenja (SAD 2020, Turska 2023, Argentina 2019), modeli izlaznosti i sastav biračkog tela (Kolumbija, Kostarika, Čile, Bolivija), kasni preokret (Alberta 2012, Brazil 2022, Holandija 2023). Nijedno od ovih objašnjenja statistika sama ne može da potvrdi ni za Ipsos 2026; to zahteva Ipsosove sirove podatke. Prikrivanje opredeljenja je, treba reći, mehanizam koji bi delovao u smeru koji je i zabeležen (telefonska anketa u polarizovanoj kampanji, potcenjena opozicija) — ali u dokumentovanim slučajevima proizvodi 5–10 poena, ne 21, i ne objašnjava zašto je svih šesnaest malih lista precenjeno. Ono što katalog pokazuje jeste da među izbornim anketama sa terenom u poslednjoj nedelji, uzorkom od dve hiljade i više, objavljenim naručiocem i neosporenim rezultatom, promašaj ove veličine **nema parnjaka u ovom katalogu**.

**Srbija 2012.** Deset dana pred drugi krug predsedničkih izbora (20. maj 2012), mediji su objavili istraživanje pripisano Ipsos Strategic Marketingu (terensko istraživanje 10. maja, n = 1.198): Tadić 58%, Nikolić 42%; drugi izveštaj iz istih dana navodi 52 prema 48. Nikolić je pobedio sa 51,2% prema 48,8% važećih glasova. Ipsos je naknadno (2021, 2022) saopštio da nikakve brojke za drugi krug nije zvanično objavio, da sopstveno istraživanje za drugi krug nije ni imao, i da je neko medijima dao podatke pod imenom Ipsosa; to je u tabeli i referencama navedeno, a obe verzije brojki prikazane su na graficima. Sa objavljenih 58/42, greška razlike je `r fmt_d_sr(rs12$absE)` poena; sa 52/48, `r fmt_d_sr(abs(E12_alt))`.

Potpuna analiza, tabela sa svim slučajevima i reference slede na engleskom.

</div>

# Introduction

## The question

On 25 October 2026 Serbia held snap parliamentary elections. The final pre-election poll by **Ipsos Strategic Marketing**, published on 22 October (fieldwork 20–22 October, n = 3,624, commissioned by the *Ujedinjena Srbija* list), had *Aleksandar Vučić – Ujedinjena Srbija* at 47.4% and *Studentska lista – Studenti pobeđuju* at 40.0%, with a stated margin of ±2.1 points.<sup><a href="#ref-rs26_ipsos">1</a></sup> The Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) counted *Studentska lista* 53.0%, *Ujedinjena Srbija* 39.0%.<sup><a href="#ref-rs26_rik">2</a></sup>

The [companion technical report](Ipsos-Izbori-2026.html) establishes that random sampling error cannot account for this: the exact multinomial probability of a random sample landing at least that far from the truth is about 2 × 10<sup>−36</sup>, and no variant of the assumptions lifts it above 10<sup>−30</sup>.<sup><a href="#ref-rs26_repo">3</a></sup> That report deliberately says nothing about *why* the gap exists.

This document asks a different, comparative question: **how large is the 2026 Ipsos miss relative to the well-documented pre-election polling failures of the last sixteen years, worldwide?** Polls miss. The literature on polling error is large, and the misses that entered the public memory — the 2015 British general election, the Brexit referendum, the US state polls of 2016 and 2020, Israel 2015, Australia 2019, the Colombian peace plebiscite — each produced inquiries and post-mortems. Putting Ipsos 2026 next to them, on a common scale, is the only way to say whether "polls miss sometimes" is an adequate description of what happened.

## What this document does and does not do

<div class="callout callout-warn">
**Read this before reading any number below.**

1. **Scope.** Final pre-election polls (published before the vote), for national or sub-national elections and referendums, worldwide, from 2010 to 2026. Exit polls, seat projections built from constituency models, and forecasting aggregators are out of scope, with one exception noted in the table (the Brexit poll of polls is reported alongside individual polls for context). Three further rules. (a) Only polls whose fieldwork ended within 16 days of the vote — the longest legal pre-election blackout among the cases (Chile) — count as final polls; an agency's last poll published five weeks out is not a final poll and is reported in the text, not the table. (b) The official count is taken as the truth, because the metric has no other anchor; elections whose official count is disputed by international observers (Venezuela 2024, Georgia 2024) are therefore excluded and listed in Section 4 with their figures. (c) A case enters the catalogue when the final poll(s) either got the winner wrong, or missed the margin between the top two by at least about five points. The five-point threshold is this document's own choice, not a figure from the literature; it is roughly twice the typical final-week error on a party share reported by Jennings & Wlezien (about 2 points), and large enough that every case in the British, American and Australian inquiries clears it.<sup><a href="#ref-jennings_wlezien">4</a></sup>
2. **One row per poll, not per election.** Where an election had many pollsters, the table lists the final poll(s) most cited in the post-mortems, so that a named agency with a published sample size can be compared with a named agency. Poll averages, where an official one exists, are mentioned in the text but are not rows.
3. **Sourcing.** Every poll figure is referenced to the agency's own release or, where that is no longer online, to a contemporaneous report of it; every official result to the electoral authority or a document reproducing its figures; every explanation to the inquiry, academic paper, pollster statement or press analysis that offered it, labelled by type. Where only a secondary source could be reached, the table says so. All links were checked on 2 November 2026.
4. **What the catalogue cannot show.** It cannot say why Ipsos 2026 missed. The explanations column records what *others* concluded about *their* misses; it is context, not diagnosis. The document makes no claim about intent in any case.
5. **It is not exhaustive.** Candidate cases that were considered and left out, and why, are listed in Section 4.
</div>

## How a miss is measured

<div class="concept">
#### Concept: margin error and standardised error

The measure used here is the **error on the margin**: take the eventual winner and the eventual runner-up (or the winning and losing option in a referendum), compute the poll's lead for the winner, compute the actual lead, and subtract. It is the headline measure of the AAPOR task-force reports on the 2016 and 2020 US polls, and one of the two measures in Jennings & Wlezien's comparative study of 351 elections, whose primary measure is the absolute error on each party's share.<sup><a href="#ref-jennings_wlezien">4</a>,<a href="#ref-us20_aapor">`r ref_num["us20_aapor"]`</a></sup>

$$E = (\hat{p}_{\text{winner}} - \hat{p}_{\text{runner-up}}) - (p_{\text{winner}} - p_{\text{runner-up}})$$

where $\hat{p}$ are the polled shares and $p$ the official shares. A negative $E$ means the poll underestimated the winner's lead; $E$ below $-(p_{\text{winner}} - p_{\text{runner-up}})$ means the poll had the wrong winner. This measure is used because it is what readers of a poll actually act on (who is ahead, and by how much), and because it is insensitive to how undecided respondents or small parties are treated, as long as the two leading options are measured on the same base.

A raw error of five points means different things for a poll of 600 respondents and a poll of 3,600. A random sample of size $n$ from a population in which the two leading options have shares $p_1, p_2$ produces a lead whose standard error is

$$\text{SE}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) = \sqrt{\frac{p_1 + p_2 - (p_1 - p_2)^2}{n}}$$

(the variance of a difference of two multinomial proportions). The **standardised error** $z = |E| / \text{SE}$ is the number of standard errors by which the poll missed, under the hypothesis that it was a simple random sample of the voting population. It is the two-category version of the test in the companion report, and is reported only where the poll's sample size is documented. Under random sampling, $|z| > 2$ happens about one time in twenty; $|z| > 4$ about one time in 16,000; $|z| > 6$ about one time in 500 million.
</div>

refs <- refs |> dplyr::mutate(num = dplyr::row_number())
ref_num <- setNames(refs$num, refs$id)
# inline citation: cite("uk15_ipsos", "uk15_result") -> <sup>11,12</sup> with anchors
cite <- function(...) {
  ids <- unlist(strsplit(paste(c(...), collapse = ";"), ";"))
  stopifnot(all(ids %in% names(ref_num)))
  paste0("<sup>", paste(sprintf('<a href="#ref-%s">%d</a>', ids, ref_num[ids]), collapse = ","), "</sup>")
}
```

## The catalogue

Each row is one final pre-election poll. `poll_w` / `poll_r` are the polled shares of the eventual winner and runner-up (or winning and losing referendum option); `act_w` / `act_r` the official shares; `n` the poll's sample size as published (NA where no primary or contemporaneous source states it). Shares are on the base the poll itself used (decided voters, valid votes, two-party-preferred, …) and the official result is taken on the same base wherever the sources allow; the `basis` column says which. For Israel 2015, where polls report seats, polled "shares" are seat shares (seats / 120).

  "Likud", "Zionist Union", 18.3, 21.7, 25.0, 20.0, "il15_polls", "il15_result",
  "<b>Academic (Fisher):</b> Likud won 30 seats against final polls of about 22–25; aggregating the right-wing bloc makes the polls look better but does not necessarily explain the discrepancy. <b>Press:</b> pollsters' comments on the (exit-poll) refusals concentrated at pro-Likud stations; the IDI's Peace Index found no change in the final week, which argues against a late swing.", "il15_fisher;il15_toi",
  "Israeli polls report seats, so both sides are seat shares: polled 22/120 and 26/120, actual 30/120 and 24/120 (on vote shares, 23.40/18.67, the error is −8.1). Legal blackout from 13 March.",

  "uk15", "2015-05-07", "UK general election", "Velika Britanija, parlamentarni izbori", "United Kingdom", "Election",

  "Conservative", "Labour", 36, 35, 37.8, 31.2, "uk15_ipsos", "uk15_result;uk15_inquiry",
  "<b>Inquiry (BPC/MRS, Sturgis et al.):</b> the primary cause was unrepresentative samples (too many Labour, too few Conservative respondents) that weighting did not correct; late swing contributed at most around one point; deliberate misreporting and “shy Tories” rejected; final-week convergence consistent with herding, not collusion.", "uk15_inquiry",
  "The poll-of-polls (Con 34, Lab 34, 12 polls) missed by 6.6.",

No formal post-mortem was published; the capital controls of 29 June preceded all final fieldwork, and Public Issue's own poll had 9% undecided and 3.5% non-voters.", "gr15_young;gr15_pi_post",
  "One of several final polls, all within three points of a tie except Metron Analysis (3 Jul: No 48, Yes 44 raw), which still missed by 18.6. Raw (undecided-inclusive) poll base against valid votes; on the allocated figures (45.5/45) the error is −22.1 as well.",

  "eu16a", "2016-06-23", "UK EU membership referendum (Brexit)", "Velika Britanija, referendum o članstvu u EU (Bregzit)", "United Kingdom", "Referendum",

  "Leave", "Remain", 45, 55, 51.9, 48.1, "eu16_populus;eu16_bpc", "eu16_result",
  "<b>Industry body (BPC):</b> every final poll overstated Remain (mean error 4.3 points); three within ±3; no formal inquiry held. <b>Industry seminar (BPC/MRS/NCRM, summarised by Atkinson):</b> turnout 72% against the ~60% most pollsters expected, with new voters splitting about 60/40 for Leave; only five of ten firms weighted by education; online did better than phone. <b>Academic (Curtice, before the vote):</b> the phone/online gap lay in sample composition, and education was not adequately accounted for.", "eu16_bpc;eu16_mrs;eu16_curtice",
  "Populus was the largest final-poll miss; the poll-of-polls (Remain 52, Leave 48) missed by 7.8. Populus's own release is no longer online; figures from the BPC table and a contemporaneous report.",

  "No", "Sí", 34, 66, 50.22, 49.78, "co16_ipsos", "co16_result",

  "The largest miss in the catalogue. Invamer (Sí 67.6) and Cifras & Conceptos (Sí 62) missed by 35.6 and 24.4. n is the likely-voter base on which 66/34 was computed.",

  "<b>Analysis (companion report, same author):</b> sampling error excluded (p ≈ 2 × 10<sup>−36</sup>); the remaining candidates — a late swing of about 450,000 voters, a turnout or undecided shift of unusual size, non-sampling bias far larger than final polls ordinarily carry, or the published numbers not reflecting what the survey measured — cannot be separated by statistics. No post-mortem by Ipsos had been found as of 2 November 2026.", "rs26_repo",
  "z is computed with n<sub>eff</sub> = 2,110, the effective sample size the companion report backs out of Ipsos's published intervals (an approximate figure: the intervals are rounded and the median across lists is used); it combines the decided base and the design effect, neither of which Ipsos published, and is the choice most favourable to Ipsos. With the nominal 3,624 interviews this document's z rises from 10.4 to 13.5. RIK's percentages are shares of all ballots found in the boxes, the base Ipsos used (list shares plus an assumed 2.5% invalid), so no rescaling is needed; the companion report's preliminary snapshot (53.03/38.97) differs by 0.02."

  dplyr::mutate(
    date   = as.Date(date),
    year   = as.integer(format(date, "%Y")),
    poll_lead   = poll_w - poll_r,
    actual_lead = act_w - act_r,
    E           = poll_lead - actual_lead,            # margin error, points (negative = winner underestimated)
    absE        = abs(E),
    wrong_winner = poll_lead < 0,
    pw = act_w / 100, pr = act_r / 100,
    se_margin = 100 * sqrt((pw + pr - (pw - pr)^2) / n),  # SE of the polled lead under random sampling, points
    z = absE / se_margin
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date, agency) |>
  dplyr::mutate(no = dplyr::row_number())
```

```{r table}
tbl <- misses |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Event = sprintf("<b>%s</b><br><span style='color:#52514e'>%s · %s</span>", event, format(date, "%d %b %Y"), type),
    n_label = ifelse(id == "rs26", "n = 3,624 published; n<sub>eff</sub> = 2,110 derived", paste0("n = ", fmt_n(n))),
    Agency = sprintf("<b>%s</b>%s<br><span style='color:#52514e'>%s · %s · %s · %s</span>",
                     agency,

                     fieldwork, mode, n_label, basis),

    Result = sprintf("%s <b>%s</b><br>%s %s<br><span style='color:#52514e'>lead %s</span>%s",
                     winner, fmt_pct(act_w), runner, fmt_pct(act_r), fmt_sgn(actual_lead),
                     purrr::map_chr(result_refs, ~ cite(.x))),
    Miss = sprintf("<b>%s</b> pts%s<br><span style='color:#52514e'>z = %s</span>",
                   fmt_sgn(E), ifelse(wrong_winner, "<br><span style='color:#eb6834'>wrong winner</span>", ""),
                   ifelse(is.na(z), "n/a", sprintf("%.1f", z))),
    Explanation = sprintf("%s%s%s", explanation, purrr::map_chr(expl_refs, ~ cite(.x)),
                          ifelse(caveat == "", "", sprintf("<br><span style='color:#898781'><i>%s</i></span>", caveat)))
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(`#` = no, Event, Agency, `Poll (final)` = Poll, `Official result` = Result, `Margin error` = Miss, `Possible explanation (type: source)` = Explanation)

kable_report(tbl, align = c("r", "l", "l", "l", "l", "r", "l"),
             caption = sprintf("Table 1. %d final pre-election poll misses, 2010–2026, in chronological order. Margin error = (polled lead of the eventual winner) − (actual lead); negative means the winner was underestimated. z = |margin error| / standard error of the lead for a random sample of the poll's size (see Section 1.3); n/a where the sample size is not documented. Superscripts link to the numbered references.", nrow(misses))) |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(1, width = "2em") |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(2, width = "13em") |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(3, width = "15em") |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(4, width = "10em") |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(5, width = "10em") |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(6, width = "6em") |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(7, width = "32em") |>
  kableExtra::row_spec(which(misses$agency_group == "Ipsos SM, Serbia (2026; 2012 attributed)"), background = "#fdf6f2")
```

```{r summary-numbers}
rs26 <- misses |> dplyr::filter(id == "rs26")
rank_abs   <- misses |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(absE)) |> dplyr::mutate(r = dplyr::row_number())
rank_abs_e <- misses |> dplyr::filter(type == "Election") |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(absE)) |> dplyr::mutate(r = dplyr::row_number())
rank_z     <- misses |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(z)) |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(z)) |> dplyr::mutate(r = dplyr::row_number())
r26_abs   <- rank_abs$r[rank_abs$id == "rs26"]
r26_abs_e <- rank_abs_e$r[rank_abs_e$id == "rs26"]
r26_z     <- rank_z$r[rank_z$id == "rs26"]
z26_nominal <- rs26$absE / (100 * sqrt((rs26$pw + rs26$pr - (rs26$pw - rs26$pr)^2) / 3624))
med_abs <- median(misses$absE[misses$id != "rs26"])
share_wrong <- mean(misses$wrong_winner)
ordinal <- function(k) paste0(k, c("th","st","nd","rd",rep("th",6))[ifelse(k %% 100 %in% 11:13, 1, k %% 10 + 1)])
top5_abs_ids <- rank_abs$id[rank_abs$r <= 5]
top5_z_ids   <- rank_z$id[rank_z$r <= 5]
both_top5    <- setdiff(intersect(top5_abs_ids, top5_z_ids), "rs26")
case_name    <- function(ids) { d <- misses[match(ids, misses$id), ]; sprintf("%s %d (%s)", d$country, d$year, short_agency(d$agency)) }
case_name_sr <- function(ids) { d <- misses[match(ids, misses$id), ]; sprintf("%s %d. (%s)", country_sr[d$country], d$year, short_agency(d$agency, sr = TRUE)) }
both_top5_txt <- if (length(both_top5)) paste(case_name(both_top5), collapse = " and ") else "none"
both_top5_sr  <- if (length(both_top5)) paste(case_name_sr(both_top5), collapse = " i ") else "nijedan"
top5_z_others <- setdiff(top5_z_ids, "rs26")
n_above15 <- sum(misses$absE > 15)
# alternative readings shown as hollow points: Serbia 2012 with the AP report (52/48); Serbia 2026 with the nominal n
rs12 <- misses |> dplyr::filter(id == "rs12")
E12_alt <- (48 - 52) - (rs12$act_w - rs12$act_r)
alt_pts <- tibble::tibble(id = c("rs12", "rs26"), E_alt = c(E12_alt, rs26$E), z_alt = c(abs(E12_alt) / rs12$se_margin, z26_nominal))
# rank text that admits ties within 0.1
z_near <- rank_z |> dplyr::filter(id != "rs26", abs(z - rs26$z) < 0.1)
z_rank_txt <- if (nrow(z_near)) sprintf("effectively tied for %s with %s", ordinal(min(r26_z, z_near$r)), paste(case_name(z_near$id), collapse = " and ")) else ordinal(r26_z)
z_rank_sr  <- if (nrow(z_near)) sprintf("praktično izjednačen na %d. mestu sa %s", min(r26_z, z_near$r), paste(case_name_sr(z_near$id), collapse = " i ")) else sprintf("%d.", r26_z)
```

# The comparison

## Raw margin error

```{r fig-margin, fig.height=9, fig.width=10, fig.cap=sprintf("Figure 1. Margin error of every poll in the catalogue, ranked by absolute value. Dot position is the signed error (negative: the eventual winner was underestimated); the bar length is its absolute value. Orange: Ipsos Strategic Marketing, Serbia (2026, and the 2012 poll attributed to it). Blue: other Ipsos entities. Grey: other agencies. Rows marked ✕ had the wrong winner. The hollow point on the 2012 row is the alternative contemporaneous report of that poll (52/48). Median absolute error of the other %d rows: %.1f points.", nrow(misses) - 1, med_abs)}
plot_df <- misses |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    label = sprintf("%s %d · %s", country, year, short_agency(agency)),
    label = ifelse(wrong_winner, paste0(label, " ✕"), label),
    label = forcats::fct_reorder(label, absE),
    agency_group = factor(agency_group, levels = names(col)[1:3])
  )

ggplot(plot_df, aes(y = label)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = E, yend = label, colour = agency_group), linewidth = 1.6, alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_point(aes(x = E, colour = agency_group), size = 3.4) +
  geom_point(data = plot_df |> dplyr::inner_join(alt_pts |> dplyr::filter(id == "rs12"), by = "id"), aes(x = E_alt), shape = 21, size = 3.4, colour = col[1], fill = "white", stroke = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#52514e", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-5, 5), colour = "#c3c2b7", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col[1:3]) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-35, 20, 5), labels = function(x) ifelse(x == 0, "0", sprintf("%+d", x))) +
  labs(x = "Margin error, points (polled lead of the eventual winner minus actual lead)", y = NULL,
       title = "How far the final poll missed the winner's margin",
       subtitle = sprintf("%d final pre-election polls, 2010–2026. Dashed lines: ±5 points. ✕ = wrong winner.", nrow(misses))) +
  theme_report() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9.5), legend.position = "top")
```

## Standardised error

```{r fig-z, fig.height=8, fig.width=10, fig.cap="Figure 2. Standardised error: the absolute margin error divided by the standard error of the polled lead for a simple random sample of the poll's published size. Only polls with a documented sample size are shown. The grey band marks z ≤ 2, the range an honest random sample stays within 19 times out of 20. For Ipsos 2026 the effective sample size of 2,110 is used (the choice most favourable to Ipsos); the hollow point on the 2026 row shows the value with the nominal n = 3,624, and on the 2012 row the value for the alternative report (52/48)."}
plot_z <- plot_df |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(z)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(label = forcats::fct_reorder(label, z))
nominal_pt <- plot_z |> dplyr::inner_join(alt_pts, by = "id") |> dplyr::mutate(z = z_alt)

ggplot(plot_z, aes(y = label)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = 2, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "#e1e0d9", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = z, yend = label, colour = agency_group), linewidth = 1.6, alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_point(aes(x = z, colour = agency_group), size = 3.4) +
  geom_point(data = nominal_pt, aes(x = z), shape = 21, size = 3.4, colour = col[1], fill = "white", stroke = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col[1:3]) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 22, 2)) +
  labs(x = "Standardised error (standard errors of a random sample of the poll's size)", y = NULL,
       title = "The same misses, scaled by what sampling error could produce",
       subtitle = "Larger samples have less excuse: a 5-point miss is z ≈ 2.5 at n = 600 and z ≈ 10 at n = 9,500.\nGrey band: z ≤ 2. Hollow points: Ipsos 2026 with the nominal n = 3,624; Serbia 2012 on the 52/48 report.") +
  theme_report() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9.5), legend.position = "top")
```

## What the comparison shows

```{r top-tables}
top_abs <- rank_abs |> dplyr::slice_head(n = 8) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Rank = r, Case = sprintf("%s %d · %s", country, year, agency), Type = type,
                   `Margin error` = fmt_sgn(E), z = ifelse(is.na(z), "n/a", sprintf("%.1f", z)))
top_z <- rank_z |> dplyr::slice_head(n = 8) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Rank = r, Case = sprintf("%s %d · %s", country, year, agency), n = fmt_n(n),
                   `Margin error` = fmt_sgn(E), z = sprintf("%.1f", z))
kable_report(top_abs, caption = "Table 2. The eight largest misses by raw margin error.")
kable_report(top_z, caption = "Table 3. The eight largest misses by standardised error (documented sample sizes only).")
```

<div class="callout callout-result">
**Where Ipsos 2026 sits.** With a margin error of **`r fmt_sgn(rs26$E)` points**, the Ipsos Strategic Marketing poll of 22 October 2026 is the **`r ordinal(r26_abs)`-largest** miss in a catalogue of `r nrow(misses)` documented final-poll failures from 16 years and `r length(unique(misses$country))` countries, and the **`r ordinal(r26_abs_e)`-largest among elections** (as opposed to referendums). Above it are two referendums in which the situation changed between fieldwork and the vote — the Colombian peace plebiscite of 2016 (Ipsos Napoleón Franco, −32.4, turnout half of what the polls assumed) and the Greek bailout referendum of 2015 (Public Issue, `r fmt_sgn(misses$E[misses$id=="gr15"])`) — and the two final polls of the Costa Rican presidential runoff of 2018: OPol (`r fmt_sgn(misses$E[misses$id=="cr18a"])`, a poll commissioned by the losing candidate's campaign, which was not disclosed at the time) and the independent CIEP-UCR (`r fmt_sgn(misses$E[misses$id=="cr18b"])`), in a race where the university's own panel study later found that 60% of first-round abstainers had turned out for the winner. The median absolute margin error of the other `r nrow(misses)-1` rows — rows selected *because* they are famous misses — is `r sprintf("%.1f", med_abs)` points; Ipsos 2026 is `r sprintf("%.1f", rs26$absE/med_abs)` times that.

On the **standardised** scale it is **`r z_rank_txt`** of `r nrow(rank_z)` with the effective sample size of 2,110 (z = `r sprintf("%.1f", rs26$z)`), and `r ordinal(1 + sum(rank_z$z[rank_z$id != "rs26"] > z26_nominal))` with the nominal 3,624 (z = `r sprintf("%.1f", z26_nominal)`). The other cases in the top five on *both* scales: `r both_top5_txt`.
</div>

**Three readings of the two charts.**

*First, the raw scale.* Most of the catalogue sits between 5 and 14 points. That band contains the misses that produced formal inquiries — the 2015 British election (−5.6 for Ipsos MORI, −6.6 for the average), Brexit (−7.8 for Ipsos MORI and the poll of polls, −13.8 for Populus), Australia 2019 (−6.1), the 2016 Wisconsin polls (−6.8), Israel 2015 (−8.4). The inquiries treated errors of this size as serious institutional failures: the British Polling Council and the Market Research Society commissioned an independent panel after 2015, AAPOR convened committees after 2016 and 2020, the Australian industry body held an inquiry after 2019.<sup><a href="#ref-uk15_inquiry">`r ref_num["uk15_inquiry"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-us20_aapor">`r ref_num["us20_aapor"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-au19_amsro">`r ref_num["au19_amsro"]`</a></sup> Above 15 points there are `r n_above15` rows. Apart from Ipsos 2026, each carries a visible explanation in its post-mortem: an electorate that changed shape between fieldwork and the vote (a turnout collapse in Colombia, a 28% undeclared bloc in Bolivia, the consolidation of the field and of first-round abstainers behind the winner in Costa Rica), capital controls imposed on the eve of fieldwork (Greece), a single online pollster at odds with every other poll in the race (Paraguay), a ten-day-old poll of disputed provenance (Serbia 2012), or a single outlier poll that still had the winner right (ABC/WaPo in Wisconsin 2020, where the average missed by 6). Ipsos 2026 has none of these on its face: fieldwork ended three days before the vote, the poll was the agency's own, it had the wrong winner, and — as Section 3.5 shows — the one independent survey published in the same month had the right one.

*Second, the standardised scale.* Dividing by the sampling standard error does two things. It pulls the large-sample polls to the top (OPol in Costa Rica at n = 3,300, AtlasIntel in Argentina 2023 at n = 9,517, Datafolha at n = 12,800), which is the point: a big sample buys precision, not accuracy, and a 9–35-point miss on a sample that size is a bias of ten standard errors or more. And it drops the small-sample misses of the US Senate races, British Columbia and the 2015 Ipsos MORI poll (n = 556–1,186) to z ≈ 1.5–4 — a different order of failure, and a reminder that the standardised scale is blind to the thing the British and Australian inquiries actually found: a bias that was small in any one poll but identical across all of them (pooling Australia's 17 final polls gives n ≈ 23,600 and a z of about 9).<sup><a href="#ref-au19_bonham">`r ref_num["au19_bonham"]`</a></sup> Ipsos 2026, at z = `r sprintf("%.1f", rs26$z)` even on the Ipsos-friendliest sample size, is in the first group. This is the two-category shadow of the companion report's result: there, with all lists and the exact multinomial tail, the equivalent figure is about 12 standard deviations on *Studentska lista* alone and a tail probability of 10<sup>−36</sup>.<sup><a href="#ref-rs26_repo">`r ref_num["rs26_repo"]`</a></sup>

*Third, what the post-mortems found, and what that does and does not say about 2026.* The explanations column converges on a short list, and it is worth stating what each would require here.

- **Unrepresentative samples that weighting did not fix** (UK 2015, Australia 2019, Brexit's education gap, AAPOR 2016 on state polls).<sup><a href="#ref-uk15_inquiry">`r ref_num["uk15_inquiry"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-au19_amsro">`r ref_num["au19_amsro"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-eu16_mrs">`r ref_num["eu16_mrs"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-us16_aapor">`r ref_num["us16_aapor"]`</a></sup> These produced errors of 3–7 points on the margin. To produce 21 points by this route, the sample would have to be skewed on a scale the inquiries never found.
- **Non-response and concealment correlated with the vote** (AAPOR 2020; KONDA 2023; the Argentine “voto vergüenza”; Israel 2015).<sup><a href="#ref-us20_aapor">`r ref_num["us20_aapor"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-tr23_konda_post">`r ref_num["tr23_konda_post"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-ar19_fornoni">`r ref_num["ar19_fornoni"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-il15_toi">`r ref_num["il15_toi"]`</a></sup> This is the mechanism a defender of the 2026 poll would reach for first, and it is directionally consistent with what happened: in a 90%-telephone survey conducted under a polarised campaign, opposition supporters declining to answer or to declare would under-measure *Studentska lista*. The documented cases cut both ways on *who* is under-declared — the incumbent in the US 2020, Turkey 2023 and Israel 2015; the opposition in Argentina 2019 and Slovakia 2023 — and the documented magnitudes are 5–10 points on the margin. Producing 21 would require concealment on a scale none of these post-mortems found, and it would not by itself explain why sixteen small lists were all overestimated.
- **Late swing after fieldwork** (Alberta 2012, Brazil 2022, Netherlands 2023, Hungary 2022).<sup><a href="#ref-ab12_thinkhq">`r ref_num["ab12_thinkhq"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-br22_chong">`r ref_num["br22_chong"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-nl23_nos">`r ref_num["nl23_nos"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-hu22_zavecz">`r ref_num["hu22_zavecz"]`</a></sup> The companion report puts a number on this: about 450,000 voters would have had to move to *Studentska lista* between 22 and 25 October for the poll to be an ordinary unlucky draw, and such a swing would not explain why the small lists were all overestimated in the same direction.<sup><a href="#ref-rs26_repo">`r ref_num["rs26_repo"]`</a></sup>
- **Turnout and the composition of the electorate** (Colombia, Costa Rica, Chile, Bolivia, Brexit).<sup><a href="#ref-co16_elcomercio">`r ref_num["co16_elcomercio"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-cr18_panel">`r ref_num["cr18_panel"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-cl22_lagos">`r ref_num["cl22_lagos"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-bo20_cedla">`r ref_num["bo20_cedla"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-eu16_mrs">`r ref_num["eu16_mrs"]`</a></sup> The misses in this group are the largest in the catalogue, and each involved a turnout the pollsters had not modelled or an undecided share above 15%; the case closest in size to Ipsos 2026 (Costa Rica 2018) is of exactly this kind. It is therefore the mechanism that deserves the most careful statement for Serbia. Turnout was 68.9% against 58.8% at the previous parliamentary election of December 2023 — about 620,000 more voters on a slightly smaller register — and against the 64.7% Ipsos itself expected.<sup><a href="#ref-rs26_rik">`r ref_num["rs26_rik"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-rs23_rik">`r ref_num["rs23_rik"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-rs26_ipsos">`r ref_num["rs26_ipsos"]`</a></sup> The relevant counterfactual for the poll is its own turnout model: relative to it, about 275,000 more people voted than Ipsos expected, and the companion report's Scenario 3 shows that even if every one of them had voted for *Studentska lista*, a further 300,000 of the voters Ipsos did sample would still have had to switch.<sup><a href="#ref-rs26_repo">`r ref_num["rs26_repo"]`</a></sup> A composition change on the Costa Rican or Colombian scale would have required a turnout error of ten points or more; Ipsos's was four.
- **Herding and polls published too early** (UK 2015, Australia 2019, Czechia, Peru).<sup><a href="#ref-uk15_inquiry">`r ref_num["uk15_inquiry"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-au19_bonham">`r ref_num["au19_bonham"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-cz21_e15">`r ref_num["cz21_e15"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-pe21_zarate">`r ref_num["pe21_zarate"]`</a></sup> Not applicable in form: Ipsos was the last poll, three days out, and the only other October survey pointed the other way.

None of this identifies the cause of the 2026 miss, and this document does not try to. What the catalogue establishes is narrower: **among election polls with fieldwork in the final week, from samples of two thousand or more, with a disclosed commissioning party and an undisputed count, an error of this size has no counterpart in this catalogue.** The two election misses that exceed it (Costa Rica 2018) were published 11–16 days before a runoff in which the field consolidated behind the winner, and the larger of them was commissioned by the losing campaign without disclosure. Resolving which, if any, of the mechanisms above operated in Serbia requires what every serious inquiry in the catalogue began by requesting: the raw data, the weighting scheme, the likely-voter model and the treatment of undecided respondents.<sup><a href="#ref-uk15_inquiry">`r ref_num["uk15_inquiry"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-au19_amsro">`r ref_num["au19_amsro"]`</a></sup>

## Serbia 2012 and 2026, side by side

```{r rs-table}
misses |> dplyr::filter(country == "Serbia") |>
  dplyr::transmute(Year = year, Event = event, Poll = sprintf("%s %s – %s %s", winner, fmt_pct(poll_w), runner, fmt_pct(poll_r)),
                   Result = sprintf("%s %s – %s %s", winner, fmt_pct(act_w), runner, fmt_pct(act_r)),
                   `Margin error` = fmt_sgn(E), n = fmt_n(n), z = sprintf("%.1f", z),
                   `Days from fieldwork to vote` = c(10, 3)) |>
  kable_report(caption = "Table 4. The two Serbian cases. For 2012 the figures are those reported by Al Jazeera Balkans; with the AP report (52/48) the margin error is −6.3.")
```

The 2012 case is included on the figures reported at the time (Tadić 58, Nikolić 42; fieldwork 10 May, n = 1,198) because those are the figures that circulated under Ipsos's name and entered the public record as "Ipsos missed in 2012".<sup><a href="#ref-rs12_aljazeera">`r ref_num["rs12_aljazeera"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-rs12_vreme2012">`r ref_num["rs12_vreme2012"]`</a></sup> They are the only version with a sample size and a fieldwork date; a second contemporaneous report gives 52/48, which would reduce the margin error to −6.3, and both are shown in the charts.<sup><a href="#ref-rs12_ap">`r ref_num["rs12_ap"]`</a></sup> Ipsos's own account, given in 2021 and 2022, is that it did not officially publish any runoff figures, that it had no runoff survey of its own, that data it collected for a client that year mostly showed a tight race, and that someone gave media data under its name.<sup><a href="#ref-rs12_bogosavljevic">`r ref_num["rs12_bogosavljevic"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-rs12_novimagazin">`r ref_num["rs12_novimagazin"]`</a></sup> That account cannot be checked against a release, because none exists. Either way the two Serbian rows differ in kind: in 2012 a disputed poll ten days out had a 16-point lead collapse in a low-turnout runoff; in 2026 the poll was Ipsos's own, published three days out with a stated margin of ±2.1, and the *Studentska lista* share alone missed by 13.0 points, six times that margin (the 95% margin on the *lead*, for the implied sample size, is about ±4 points, and the lead missed by 21, roughly five such margins).

## The other Serbian polls of 2026

A single poll can be an outlier or part of a pattern, and the two are judged differently: the Wisconsin 2020 poll was one firm's outlier against an average that missed by 6; the British polls of 2015 all missed together. Which was Ipsos 2026? In October 2026 exactly one other agency published voting-intention figures, and three earlier estimates exist.<sup><a href="#ref-rs26_roundup">`r ref_num["rs26_roundup"]`</a></sup>

```{r other-rs-polls}
rik_lead <- rs26$act_w - rs26$act_r
other_rs <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Source, ~Published, ~Fieldwork, ~n, ~Base, ~SL, ~US, ~refs,
  "NSPM (own expense)",                 "20 Oct 2026", "25 Sep–5 Oct 2026", 1050, "decided voters (18.3% undecided excluded)", 44.5, 42.7, "rs26_nspm",
  "Ipsos Strategic Marketing (for the Ujedinjena Srbija list)", "22 Oct 2026", "20–22 Oct 2026", 3624, "decided voters, incl. 2.5% assumed invalid", 40.0, 47.4, "rs26_ipsos",
  "Faktor plus (commissioner not stated; via Blic)", "21 Sep 2026", "16–20 Sep 2026", 986, "those who would vote", 37.1, 48.6, "rs26_faktor",
  "CRTA / Stanford DAL (own)",          "15 Jul 2026", "10–24 Jun 2026", 2324, "decided voters, face-to-face", 44.9, 35.7, "rs26_crta",
  "BIRODI forecast model (not a survey)", "30 Aug 2026", "model on RIK results and published polls", NA, "valid votes", 48.5, 38.6, "rs26_birodi"
) |> dplyr::mutate(E = (SL - US) - rik_lead,
                   days = c(20, 3, 35, 123, NA))
other_rs |>
  dplyr::transmute(Source = paste0(Source, purrr::map_chr(refs, cite)), Published, Fieldwork, n = fmt_n(n), Base,
                   `Studentska lista` = fmt_pct(SL), `Ujedinjena Srbija` = fmt_pct(US),
                   `Lead` = fmt_sgn(SL - US), `Margin error vs RIK` = fmt_sgn(E),
                   `Days from end of fieldwork to vote` = ifelse(is.na(days), "", days)) |>
  kable_report(caption = sprintf("Table 5. Every published pre-election estimate for the Serbian parliamentary election of 25 October 2026, against RIK's lead of %s points. Only the Ipsos row meets the catalogue's fieldwork rule (within 16 days of the vote).", fmt_sgn(rik_lead)))
```

Every estimate understated *Studentska lista*'s lead, so 2026 is not a lone-outlier case; but the magnitudes separate sharply. The civic-sector estimates (CRTA in June, the BIRODI model in August) were within five points of the eventual margin. NSPM, polling at its own expense in late September and early October, had the winner right and the lead 12.2 points short, with 18% undecided excluded. The two polls that had the wrong winner were the two with a party connection or an undisclosed commissioner: Faktor plus, five weeks out, missed by 25.5, and Ipsos, three days out with the largest sample and the only published margins of error, by `r sprintf("%.1f", rs26$absE)`.<sup><a href="#ref-rs26_nspm">`r ref_num["rs26_nspm"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-rs26_faktor">`r ref_num["rs26_faktor"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-rs26_crta">`r ref_num["rs26_crta"]`</a>,<a href="#ref-rs26_birodi">`r ref_num["rs26_birodi"]`</a></sup> The pattern is therefore closer to Costa Rica 2018 (an independent poll short by 22 and a campaign-commissioned one short by 35) than to Britain 2015 (every firm short by the same 5–7), and it does not fit the Wisconsin 2020 pattern of one firm against an accurate field. What distinguishes Ipsos within the Serbian set is that it is the poll with the most recent fieldwork and the largest sample, and that only Faktor plus, five weeks out, had a larger error.

# Caveats

1. **Selection.** The catalogue is a list of well-documented failures, assembled from the post-mortem literature and a search of national cases in six languages, not a random sample of polls and not a census of misses: a miss in a country whose polling and results are poorly documented online will be missing here. It therefore says nothing about how often polls miss; Jennings & Wlezien's 351-election dataset puts the typical final-week absolute error at about 2 points on a party's share (they report no final-week figure for the margin).<sup><a href="#ref-jennings_wlezien">`r ref_num["jennings_wlezien"]`</a></sup> What it does allow is a like-for-like comparison of magnitudes among the misses that were large enough to be investigated.
2. **One poll per row.** Choosing which final poll represents an election is a judgement, and the ranking below the top four depends on it: Publicus for Hungary 2022 (−19.7) or Forum's 21 April poll for Alberta (−18.7) would move into ranks 6–8; Invamer for Colombia (−35.6) or Metron Analysis for Greece (−18.6) would not change the top. Where an agency published more than one final-week poll, the table uses the later one even when it missed by less (Alberta, Hungary). The caveat column gives the alternatives wherever the choice matters.
3. **Bases.** Polls publish shares on different bases (decided voters, valid votes, two-party-preferred, seats, raw figures including undecided). The margin error is insensitive to which base is used *as long as poll and result are on the same one*; where a poll's figures include an undecided share of u% and the result does not, the polled lead is understated by a factor of 1/(1−u), which for the rows concerned (Greece 2015, Alberta 2012, Argentina 2023, Bolivia 2020) moves E by one to two points — never enough to change a row's position by more than one or two places, and never the top three. The table says which base each row uses; Israel's seats are compared with seats, and the Serbian 2026 shares are on RIK's all-ballots base, which Ipsos also used.
4. **Sample sizes.** Two rows have no documented n and no z. The standardised error assumes simple random sampling with the published n. Real design effects (from weighting, clustering, or non-probability online recruitment) differ by pollster and mode and are not published, so every z here is an upper bound of unknown looseness, and rows whose z values are within a factor of about 1.5 of each other should not be read as ordered. The 2026 row is the one case where a design effect *is* applied, because Ipsos's published intervals allow it to be backed out; that works in Ipsos's favour.
5. **Secondary sources.** Where an agency's release is no longer online, the figures come from a contemporaneous report or a compiled table that cites it; each such case is marked in the table and in the reference. Four official results (Israel 2015, Hungary 2022, Peru 2021, Paraguay 2023) rest on documents reproducing the electoral authority's figures because the authority's own page could not be read. The Serbia 2012 poll rests entirely on media reports and is disputed by Ipsos.
6. **Explanations.** The explanation column reports what inquiries, researchers, pollsters or journalists concluded about *their* case, labelled by type. Inquiry and academic findings carry more weight than pollster self-assessments, which carry more weight than press analyses. None of them is a finding about Serbia 2026.
7. **The 2026 result** is RIK's count from all 8,392 polling stations as read on 2 November 2026 (after the repeat voting of 1 November); RIK's final report with absolute totals had not been published at that time. Re-enter the final figures in the data chunk and re-knit if they differ. The companion reports use RIK's preliminary count of 31 October 2026 (8,339 of 8,392 stations; Studentska lista 53.03%, Ujedinjena Srbija 38.97%), which gives a margin error of −21.5 rather than −21.4; the difference does not change any conclusion or rank here.
8. **Self-citation.** The companion report cited for the 2026 row is by the author of this document.

# References {#references}

Every poll figure, official result and explanation in Table 1 cites one or more of the numbered entries below by superscript. Type labels: *Poll* (the agency's release or a contemporaneous report of it), *Result* (electoral authority or a document reproducing its figures), *Inquiry* (official or industry post-mortem), *Academic*, *Pollster* (the agency's own statement), *Press*, *Analysis*. All links were checked on 2 November 2026; where a site was unreachable at that time the entry says what was used instead.

```{r reflist, results='asis'}

              refs$id[i], refs$num[i], refs$type[i], refs$text[i], refs$url[i], refs$url[i]))
}
cat('</ol>\n')
